chunks: Name some computer architectures. The question: Name some computer architectures.
A computer architecture is the overall design of a processor: how it organizes memory, which instructions it understands, and how it carries them out.
Many designs exist because jobs differ. A coin-cell sensor and a data-center server both run instructions, but they need very different trade-offs in speed, power and cost.
Think of vehicles: a bicycle, a car, a bus and a freight train. None is best. Each trades cost, speed, capacity and fuel for a different job. Processor designs work the same way.
A small, simple core sips power, a big complex one is fast, and a graphics chip moves huge amounts of data at once but is slow at any single task.
In a von Neumann machine, instructions and data share one memory port, so an instruction fetch and a data access cannot happen in the same cycle. Harvard separates them.
Real CPUs mimic Harvard at the L1-cache level (split I-cache and D-cache) while presenting one unified memory above that.
Instruction set (ISA): the list of basic commands a processor understands, such as add ("What is an ISA?") Von Neumann: instructions and data share one memory and one path.
Harvard: separate memories and paths for instructions and data. RISC / CISC: a small set of simple instructions versus a large set of complex ones ("RISC vs CISC advantages").
SIMD: one instruction working on many data items at once.
Compare von Neumann and Harvard. Suppose 30% of instructions also read or write data. In a von Neumann machine, each instruction needs 1 memory access to be fetched, plus 0.
3 on average for data. That is 1. 3 accesses per instruction through one door, so it can never do better than 1. 3 cycles per instruction.
A Harvard machine has two doors and does both in the same cycle.
Real CPUs get this benefit by keeping two small, fast memories (caches) next to the core, one for instructions and one for data.
That is the whole idea: each name is a different trade-off.
"I'd split them up. By memory: von Neumann, with one shared memory for code and data, and Harvard, with separate ones; real CPUs are modified Harvard with split L1 caches.
By instruction set: CISC like x86 and RISC like ARM, RISC-V and MIPS.
By execution style: in-order pipelined, superscalar out-of-order, VLIW, SIMD/vector, GPU-style SIMT, and multicore. Then special-purpose ones like DSPs and neural accelerators.
Each one targets a bottleneck: memory bandwidth, instruction throughput, or energy per operation."
